opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think a lot of what we currently treat as matters of taste or opinion are really cases where the evidence is hard to gather and hard to process, and so people fall back on intuition, tribal affiliation, or whoever sounds most confident. Advanced AI could change that quite dramatically.

Take forecasting. Questions like "will this economic policy reduce unemployment?" or "how likely is this conflict to escalate?" get treated as ideological disputes. But they're empirical questions about the future. Once you have AI systems that can make very large numbers of forecasts, get scored against what actually happens, and build up a verifiable track record, you can see who, or what, is reliably right. We already see that human superforecasters beat pundits. AI systems could do that at enormous scale, across many domains, at low cost.

Then there are areas that seem even more subjective: how good is this scientific paper, how promising is this research direction, how trustworthy is this person's testimony. Much of that can be grounded too. You can check which judgments predict replication, which research bets pay off, which claims hold up under later scrutiny. With enough training data and feedback, AI can get much better than humans at these assessments, and show its work in a way you can audit.

The deeper potential is in helping people with disagreements that are partly about values. Often what looks like a values dispute is mostly about facts, or about what people would conclude after more reflection and more information. An AI advisor that you have good reason to trust, because it has been tested and has a track record, could help you work out what you'd actually believe if you'd thought it through carefully, considered the strongest arguments on each side, and knew the relevant facts. That could improve policy debates, help negotiators find deals both sides prefer, and reduce the extent to which politics is driven by misinformation and motivated reasoning.

Of course, this cuts both ways. The same capabilities could be used for persuasion and manipulation, or concentrated in a few hands. So a lot depends on whether we build institutions that let people verify these systems' honesty and accuracy for themselves, rather than just trusting whoever controls them. But if we get that right, I think the scope for better collective judgment is one of the most underrated upsides of advanced AI.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could ground judgments in domains often treated as subjective, including forecasting, scientific quality, research promise, and testimony, using evidence and feedback.

r002.rationale: It describes ideological disputes shaped by intuition and tribal affiliation that concern empirical questions about future outcomes.

r003.rationale: It says AI could show its work for auditing and discusses verifying systems’ honesty and accuracy.

r004.rationale: The response discusses testing AI and building institutions to verify it, but does not suggest AI is easier than humans to incentivize to behave in particular ways.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a huge amount of territory that we currently file under "that's just a matter of taste" or "reasonable people disagree" where actually a lot of the disagreement is driven by differences in information, differences in reasoning quality, and plain old errors and biases, rather than by genuinely different values at the bottom.

Take something like forecasting. Twenty years ago, if you asked whether some policy would work, you'd get a bunch of pundits with confident opinions, and it was treated as a matter of political judgement who you believed. Then Tetlock comes along and shows that you can actually score these things, and that most of the confident people are terrible at it, and that there are systematic methods that do much better. The subjective judgement turned out to have a large objective core once someone bothered to measure it.

I think advanced AI pushes that dynamic across an enormous range of domains. Because the thing about AI systems is you can run them millions of times, you can check them against outcomes, you can train them to be calibrated, and you can have them show their work. So questions like "will this intervention actually help people," "is this argument sound," "what would this person want if they understood their situation better," which today get resolved by whoever is most persuasive or has the most status in the room, could instead be resolved by systems with demonstrated track records that everyone across the political spectrum can verify.

And that extends to ethics and policy. A lot of what looks like moral disagreement is really disagreement about empirical facts, about what the consequences will be, who gets hurt, whether the thing works at all. If you strip those out, you often find the remaining value disagreement is much narrower than people thought. AI that is extremely good at the empirical and inferential parts can shrink the space of apparent subjectivity dramatically.

Then there's the part about helping people understand their own values. Humans are quite inconsistent. We hold views that contradict each other, we haven't thought through the implications, we'd change our minds given more reflection. An AI advisor that knows you very well, that can lay out "here's what you'd conclude if you thought about this for a thousand hours," could make individual and collective decision making far more coherent than it is now, without the AI imposing its own values. It's more like giving everyone a really good staff of advisors who are honest, who aren't trying to manipulate you, and who are checked for accuracy.

The big caveat, of course, is that all of this depends on the systems actually being honest and well aligned, and on the institutions around them being set up so that the verification is real rather than theatre. If you have AI that's very persuasive but not very truthful, you get the opposite effect: subjective judgement gets captured rather than clarified. So I'd say the overlooked potential is enormous, but it's contingent on getting the trustworthiness piece right, and that's a lot of why I think the alignment and epistemics work matters so much.

r001.rationale: It says advanced AI could bring objectively assessable knowledge to many areas now treated as taste or subjective judgment.

r002.rationale: It attributes some apparent disagreement to human errors and biases, and says many moral and policy disputes turn on empirical facts and consequences.

r003.rationale: It says AI can show its work and have a verifiable track record, enabling people to check how reliable its judgments are.

r004.rationale: It mentions training AI for calibration and the need for alignment, but does not say AI may be easier than humans to incentivize to behave in particular ways.

astra-6.text:
I think people often move too quickly from “this involves subjective judgement” to “there isn’t much that intelligence can do to help.” Even when there isn’t a single objectively correct answer, there can be an enormous amount to learn about what people value, why they disagree, and what would happen under different choices.

Take choosing a career. There’s no career that’s best independently of your preferences. But you might be uncertain about what the work is actually like, how you’d respond to it, or whether your current enthusiasm would survive experience. A sufficiently capable AI could help you understand those things much better. It could distinguish disagreements about what you want from mistaken predictions about what would satisfy you.

And something similar applies to moral and political judgement. Some disagreements really are differences in values, but others depend on factual beliefs, inconsistent reasoning, or having considered only a small fraction of the possible options. AI could help expose those distinctions and find arrangements that people with different values would all prefer.

That doesn’t mean treating the AI’s judgement as authoritative. You’d want to distinguish helping someone think from persuading them to adopt a particular conclusion. But there’s potentially a very large space between leaving people with their current, often poorly informed judgements and having a machine dictate what they ought to value.

r001.rationale: The response identifies career, moral, and political judgment as areas where AI could help people learn about preferences, factual beliefs, and the consequences of choices.

r002.rationale: It says disagreements can involve factual beliefs or inconsistent reasoning, but does not identify human biases as a source of conflicting answers.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss AI being more transparent than humans or using transparency to verify how AI operates.

r004.rationale: The response does not suggest that AI would be easier than humans to incentivize to behave in particular ways.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people often move too quickly from “this involves subjective judgement” to “there’s not much that greater intelligence can contribute.” Even where there isn’t a uniquely correct answer, there can be a huge amount of factual uncertainty about what we would actually prefer if we understood the situation better.

Take choosing a career, or deciding what sort of society you’d like to live in. You don’t know what all the alternatives would feel like. You don’t know how your preferences would change with experience. And you may be relying on beliefs about the consequences that are simply mistaken. An advanced AI could help you explore those possibilities, identify inconsistencies, and understand the tradeoffs much more clearly.

Similarly, in art, the fact that people have different tastes doesn’t mean there’s no skill in making something that a particular person will find beautiful or moving. Understanding that person and creating something that speaks to them can be an extremely demanding intellectual task.

So I’d distinguish between an AI discovering some objectively correct set of values and an AI helping us do a much better job of understanding and pursuing our values. The second could be enormously important without assuming the first is possible. And of course, you’d want that process to help people reflect, rather than just making them easier to persuade.

r001.rationale: The response says advanced AI could help in subjective areas such as career and societal choices by reducing factual uncertainty and clarifying tradeoffs.

r002.rationale: It mentions mistaken beliefs and inconsistencies, but does not say that conflicting answers driven by human biases can concern questions with factual answers.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss AI transparency or verifying how AI operates.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest AI may be easier than humans to incentivize toward particular behavior.
